headline: South Korea gives 52M people free, unlimited AI, but 80% must be domestic models
summary: The "AI for All" program, launching by year-end, provides free, unlimited generative AI access to all 52 million South Koreans. However, a key policy mandates that 80% of queries must be routed to domestic AI models.
details: South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT has finalized three operating consortiums (SK Telecom, KT, Kakao) for its "AI for All" program. Beta starts in September, with a full launch by year-end, offering free, unlimited generative AI access to all 52 million citizens with no token limit.

The government has allocated 512 NVIDIA B200 chips for this year, and from 2027, the national budget will partially cover the service's operational costs. This initiative makes South Korea the first G20 country to implement such a nationwide AI program.

While officially "unlimited," physical realities suggest tiered rate limiting or reliance on lightweight models will be necessary to serve 52 million users with the initial compute resources. The true extent of "unlimited" access will likely be tested.

A critical, often overlooked rule mandates that each operator must route at least 50% of queries to its own "certified Korean sovereign foundation model" and another 30% to other Korean companies' models. This sets an 80% floor for domestic AI model usage.

This policy transforms "free and unlimited" access into an industrial strategy. The government provides compute, funding, and a massive user base, but in return, the AI used must predominantly be Korean.

From an engineering standpoint, this 80% quota aligns with cost-saving measures. Repetitive, trivial requests can be offloaded to cheaper domestic small language models (SLMs), conserving compute and helping fund the free tier.

This move positions Korea uniquely within the global "sovereign AI" trend, where countries are investing over $100 billion by 2026. Most nations focus on building supply-side infrastructure like data centers and training models.

Korea, however, is attacking the demand side. Recognizing that domestic models struggle to compete with established platforms like ChatGPT for user habits, the government is actively funneling citizens into the domestic AI ecosystem to ensure massive, everyday usage.

headline_marked: [[White House pulls 'Build the Wall' game]] after Tetris Company copyright complaint
headline: White House pulls 'Build the Wall' game after Tetris Company copyright complaint
summary: The game, widely criticized as racist, closely mimicked Tetris gameplay, tasking players with stacking blocks to build a border wall against a "zombie border siege."
details: A video game posted to the Trump administration’s website, which closely resembled Tetris, has been taken down. This removal occurred after the Tetris Company officially lodged a complaint.

The game, titled 'Build the Wall,' was one of several arcade-style games recently added to the White House site. It was widely criticized as racist for its stated goal of building a wall to keep out a 'zombie border siege.'
The page for 'Build the Wall' now displays a 404 error, confirming its removal. Kotaku was the first to report the game's disappearance from the government website.

The Trump administration has been reached out to for comment by TechCrunch. Another controversial game, 'Rio Run,' which involves deporting immigrant characters, remains accessible on the government's website.
